lesson.title: Reviewing two-step equations
lesson.skill: Recall the rule that keeps an equation true, without looking it up.
lesson.missionLink: You are close to the Friday deadline. This is the check that tells you whether the two lessons before it stuck.

primarySource.why: Worth one more read if the recall below comes back empty.

content.text: Answer from memory first. Looking back at lesson three afterwards is how you find out what you actually kept.

blocks.text: What this lesson does not repeat

content.text: A review introduces no new explanation. If something here is unfamiliar, it belongs to an earlier lesson, not to this one.
Getting a recall answer roughly right counts. The point is to find the gaps, not to pass.

blocks.text: Pick your way back to it

questions.prompt: Which step comes first when you solve 2x + 3 = 11?

options.feedback: That is the second move. It only works once the 3 is off both sides.
Exactly that. Take the 3 off first and the term x is left standing alone.
You cannot divide yet, because there is still a 3 sitting on top of x.

questions.explanation: Undo addition before you undo multiplication. Doing it the other way round changes what the 2 is multiplying.

questions.prompt: Your answer does not check out when you put it back in. What do you check first?

options.feedback: Yes. Every step has to be reversible, or the equation changed meaning somewhere.
Whether the answer is a whole number is worth knowing, but it comes after this.
They should match. If they do not, the mistake is earlier than the last line.

questions.explanation: Check that every step was reversible, then put the answer back on both sides.

blocks.text: Now say it back, from memory

blocks.prompt: In your own words, why do you undo addition before you undo multiplication?
blocks.modelAnswer: Addition was applied last, so it is undone first. Undoing multiplication first would change what the coefficient multiplies.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, what makes a step reversible?
blocks.modelAnswer: A step is reversible when it does the same operation to both sides with something other than zero, so you can always undo it and get the original equation back.
rubric: Not multiplying or dividing by zero

blocks.prompt: In your own words, what do you do when both sides stop matching?
blocks.modelAnswer: Go back through the steps and find the first one that was not applied to both sides, then redo from there.
rubric: Checks each step was applied to both sides
Redoes the work from the first bad step
